slides.title: Picking a meal is easy; sizing it to you is not
slides.subtitle: Three questions sit between a craving and a meal you can trust.
slides.takeaway: The Today lines are this project's framing of the problem, not survey results.

notes.purpose: Show the work that sits between a craving and a meal.
script: Most of us know what we feel like eating. The hard part comes after that.
The right amount depends on the person. Diets and conditions change the meal. And even one meal means several ingredients to find and price.
The next section shows how one request answers all three.

slides.title: From your body to a meal target
slides.subtitle: Worked example: an active woman keeping her weight. Her meal target is 28% of the daily budget.
slides.takeaway: The model's R² of 0.996 is for exercise calories only, which add just 3–10% of the day in these plans.
slides.question: How does it decide how much?

notes.purpose: Follow one person from body to meal target.
script: Body size and activity give about 2,344 kcal a day. The trained model adds 125. Her goal is to maintain, so her budget is 2,469, and one meal gets 28%: 691 kcal.
Exercise adds only 5% here because the run uses default exercise inputs: 30 minutes at 100 bpm.
A weight-loss floor of 1,200 kcal for women and 1,500 for men protects low budgets.
Sources: calorie_expenditure_agent.py; models/calorie_expenditure/metrics.json; local run, 7 November 2026.

notes.purpose: Appendix: what the workout check measured and the two fixes it led to.
script: The fixed 72 requests send no workout. This check sends six: not given, rest day, a walk, a jog, a run and a ride, for each of the four profiles on six cravings.

The activity level already holds an average day's exercise: 626 kcal for this man. Before the fix, today's workout was added on top on 15 of 24 profile-days. Now a stated workout replaces it, so his run day falls from 3,251 to 2,625 kcal. A workout left out still adds the 30-minute default to the activity level.

The model was trained on 1 to 30 minutes, so 60 and 90 minutes used to count as 30. They now count per minute. Heart rates above 128 bpm are still read as 128, and every request uses the 37 °C body-temperature default, which is just below the training range.
The one miss: targets between about 360 and 390 kcal push Tuna Pasta Salad's carbs to 43%, because the pasta cannot shrink below half a portion.
Sources: docs/7_meal_quality.md §5 (Workout days); docs/meal_quality/workouts.md; DEC-39, DEC-40; PR #57.

notes.purpose: Appendix: the first benchmark run with independent nutrition data, and what it found.
script: The same 72 requests, with each ingredient's nutrition from USDA FoodData Central instead of the local tables. Nineteen ingredients with a trusted local value are never sent. USDA search results are live, so this run is not repeatable and never replaces the offline benchmark.

The first run read energy in kilojoules for foods that list both units: shrimp came out at 356 kcal per 100 g instead of 85. With that fixed, every plan is back within 10% of its calories, and 50 of 72 meet both targets; the median gap is 0.7%.

Almost every remaining miss has calories on target and fat too high, because the lookup takes USDA's first search hit: avocado finds avocado dressing, and lean turkey mince finds minced ham. The ham match alone causes 16 of the 22 misses, through the fallback turkey bowl.
Next: pin one reviewed USDA food per ingredient in the reference data, so the lookup is repeatable, then rerun.
Sources: docs/7_meal_quality.md §6 (With USDA data), DEC-41; docs/meal_quality/usda_baseline.md, usda_wider.md, usda_lookup_diagnosis.md; PR #59.
